_comment: What clawd-light consumes from Claude Code, as data.
One entry per hook event, listing the payload fields the app actually reads.
The check asserts PRESENCE of what we consume, never absence of what we don't:
Claude Code adding a field is not a breakage, removing one is.
Every entry here has a matching record in assumptions.md that says where we
depend on it and what breaks if it goes away.
These fire only under conditions a probe cannot force cheaply.
They stay under unit test with recorded shapes; the live probe skips them
and says so, rather than passing silently.
The session transcript: a JSONL file whose path arrives in every hook
payload as `transcript_path`. It is what the chat window renders.
Unlike the hook payloads, this one can be checked for free and at scale:
the files are already on disk, by the thousand. The check samples the most
recent ones and asserts the invariants below still hold.
The load-bearing one is `humanOrigin`. A transcript record of type `user`
is USUALLY not a human message — it is a tool result. On this machine the
ratio was 1683 tool results to 119 real prompts. Telling them apart by
anything other than `origin.kind` means rendering tool output as if the
user had typed it.

extensionPatterns._comment: Substrings that must still be present in the VS Code extension bundle.

_comment: Patterns whose DISAPPEARANCE is good news, not a breakage.
The extension currently refuses to apply a prompt to a session whose panel
is already open, and says so to the user. That single refusal is what makes
the Codex-style 'act on the running agent' features unreachable — see
decision N7. If it ever goes away, the door opens.
The checker reports these separately and never fails on them.
The mechanism that carries a message from the chat window into a running
session: a second Stop hook marked asyncRewake, spawned detached, whose
stdout becomes the message and whose exit code 2 sends it.
These option names are @internal in Claude Code. They can be renamed
without deprecation, and when they are, the feature stops working in
SILENCE: no error, no log, the message simply never arrives. That is the
worst failure shape there is, and it is the entire reason this section
exists. The check greps the shipped binary for the names.
Verified by reproduction on 2026-08-01: an idle session, a message written
from an unrelated process, a full turn with tool use 30 seconds later.
The list of in-flight background work carried by Stop, and the reason a
session that is still working does not go green.
The load-bearing part is not the field's presence but its FILTERING:
Claude Code drops anything that is neither running nor pending, and
anything not backgrounded, before it builds the array. Because of that,
presence in the list is the signal and the status word is only a
backstop. If that filter loosened without us noticing, finished tasks
would start arriving and every affected row would stay yellow for ever.
The opposite drift is worse and quieter: if the field vanished, or the
statuses were renamed wholesale, every turn would look clean and the
green-during-work lie returns with nothing to report it.
This check exists because of tmux, which keeps the same kind of table of
what an undocumented dependency actually does — and has no test that any
of it is still true.
notWorkTypes mirrors Claude Code's own active-tasks view, which drops
remote_agent and dream after applying the payload filter. If activeViewFilterPattern
stops matching the binary, Claude Code changed its mind about what counts as work
and so must we - in either direction.
Every hook event name Claude Code knows about, and why we do or do not
use it.
This list exists because the contract used to say 'the eight events',
which reads as 'these are the events'. There are thirty-one. Nothing
would have told us if a thirty-second appeared, or if one we register
were renamed out from under us.
The classification below distinguishes what was MEASURED from what was
only read in the binary — the distinction that matters, because reading
a name out of the enum and inferring its meaning is exactly how
TaskCreated got recommended for a job it does not do.

decodedButNotRegistered._why: Mapped to `working` if it ever arrives. Not registered: it would fire on every tool call and cannot release a pending question, because it carries permissionDecision in its own output and therefore runs before the prompt, not after the answer.

decisionHooks._why: These do not observe, they answer. Their output schema carries a verdict — PermissionRequest returns decision.behavior allow|deny, Elicitation returns action accept|decline|cancel — so a hook registered here sits inside the approval path. Measured in the binary's output schema; NOT measured live, because a non-interactive `claude -p` never reaches an approval prompt. Registering one changes clawd-light from something that watches into something that can decide, and that is a posture change, not a fix.

teammateBoard._why: MEASURED, and not what the names suggest. The payload is task_id, task_subject, task_description, teammate_name, team_name: the teammates/team task board, unrelated to background shells. A probe that ran a real backgrounded `sleep 6` produced neither of them.

notAboutTurnState._why: Workspace and editor facts, not what a session is doing. Read in the binary, never probed.
